Lives

{{W_LIVES_CAP}} people whose influence outlasted them, and the one book on each worth your time. {{W_FAMOUS_CAP}} the world remembers; {{N_OBSCURE}} it forgot but shouldn't. Reading lives at volume is the cheapest way to borrow judgment you have not yet earned — a board of directors you will never meet. Every pick carries a note on where specialists would argue with it, because "definitive" is a claim, not a fact. Each is numbered: the founding shelf first, then every life since in the order it joined, and a number never changes.

The Atlas

Founders, coaches, investors, a lion tracker, a surgeon: what each of them taught me, from the notes I take while listening. I chart them as sources and pass no verdict on them.

The method

This is a library, not a credential. It holds what I have read, what I think it means, and — deliberately, in every wing — the places where the people who know most still disagree. A claim without its dispute is half a claim.

The two wings are one method applied to people, two ways round. Lives is the people themselves, one book each; The Atlas is the people I listen to now, and the principles I hear more than one of them teach. The library used to run to five wings — a set of field manuals and a trade book of operating lessons. Both were positions stated without anyone standing behind them, and they came down in September 2026 so that everything here is attached to a person you can go and check. A third, the Press — {{N_BOOKS}} titles on the ideas people spent their lives inside — was retired on 14 October 2026. Nothing in it was withdrawn as wrong: its titles keep their own pages, with their sources, their disputes and their corrections, for anyone who holds a link, and the contents still lists them.

Set in EB Garamond and IBM Plex Mono. Assembled by hand and with AI assistance; figures are checked against a named source, and where I have corrected myself the correction stays visible rather than being quietly patched. The reading wings are set on paper. The Atlas is the only room kept dark: it is drawn as a sea chart, the one room here that is a map rather than a page, and a chart is read by lamplight.

The portraits in Lives are public-domain engravings, paintings and photographs, reduced to the house duotone and set as plates. A life without a safely public image carries the press mark instead of a borrowed picture, which seems the more honest trade. {{W_PLATELESS_CAP}} lives are in that position today. Henrietta Lacks is there by decision; her entry says why at length, and her estate has itself disputed the use of family photographs. The rest are there because no image of them has yet been cleared. Clair Patterson's photographs sit in an archive that grants permission only on request. No photograph of Alice Ball has been found under any licence we can stand behind. Edward Thorp and Larry Gagosian are alive and photographed by working photographers, whose pictures are theirs. The 1939 Los Angeles Times portrait of Hedy Lamarr is tagged elsewhere as openly licensed, while the library that holds it says, for that collection, that permission to publish must be asked for in writing. The only photographs of Chester Carlson the house has found are held by Xerox or by the archives of his papers, or printed on a postage stamp, and none comes with a licence we can stand behind. The one portrait of Kelly Johnson tagged as a government work is a 1970s portrait of a Lockheed vice-president that the CIA reproduced, most likely a company photograph rather than the agency's own. The one openly licensed portrait of Claude Shannon is licensed by a Swedish museum that names neither the photographer nor the date, so its right to grant the licence is asserted rather than shown. The only Library of Congress portrait catalogued under Henry J. Kaiser's name shows a young army corporal, not the industrialist, while the Truman Library offers its photograph of him at the user's own risk. The photograph of Akio Morita from the São Paulo state government's archive, taken in 1972 and public domain in Brazil, carries no statement of its status in the United States; the others found are under a United States copyright restored in 1996 or too small to print. The portraits of Levi Strauss in circulation trace to a fashion blog, a stock-certificate dealer and an undated upload, with no photographer, date or publication recorded for any of them, and the company's own prints come with no licence. The portraits of Milton Hershey in circulation come from the Hershey Community Archives with a public-domain tag supplied by the uploader and no photographer or publication recorded. The Library of Congress print of Howard Hughes is a Wide World Photos agency picture whose rights the Library has not evaluated. No public-domain portrait of Malcom McLean has been found; the one openly licensed photograph names no photographer and its source page is gone. For Rose Blumkin and Henry Singleton the house has no record of a search yet. Where no likeness can be used but something from the life can, the plate shows that instead, a manuscript page or a boat, and says so under the picture. {{W_CCPLATES_CAP}} plates are licensed rather than public domain, and are credited here because the licence requires it: the Mandela photograph is by South Africa The Good News (sagoodnews.co.za) under CC BY 2.0; the Steve Jobs photograph was taken at WWDC in 2010 by Matthew Yohe under CC BY-SA 3.0; the Tu Youyou photograph was taken in Stockholm on 6 December 2015 by Bengt Nyman under CC BY-SA 4.0; the 1955 photograph of Rosalind Franklin at her microscope is credited to the MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology, from the personal collection of her sister Jenifer Glynn, under CC BY-SA 4.0; the photograph of Samuel Zemurray, taken on 10 January 1934 for the Los Angeles Times, is from the Los Angeles Times Photographic Collection at UCLA Library Special Collections, under CC BY 4.0; the autochrome of Ivar Kreuger, taken on 8 March 1930 by Georges Chevalier, is from the musée Albert-Kahn, Département des Hauts-de-Seine (A74890), under CC BY 4.0; the 1973 photograph of David Geffen under the Roxy marquee is by Tony Barnard for the Los Angeles Times, from the Los Angeles Times Photographic Collection at UCLA Library Special Collections, under CC BY 4.0; the Kobe Bryant photograph was taken at the Lakers’ game in Washington on 3 December 2014 by Keith Allison under CC BY-SA 2.0; the James Dyson photograph was taken on 29 August 2011 by Nobuyuki Hayashi under CC BY 2.0; and the 2010 photograph of Charlie Munger is by Nick Webb under CC BY 2.0. Each has been cropped and reduced to the house duotone, which the licences ask us to say. {{W_NARROW_CAP}} more are neither plain public domain nor licensed but held under a narrower claim, and the claim is worth repeating in the holder's own words: the 1939 photograph of Robert Moses is by C. M. Stieglitz for the New York World-Telegram & Sun, held by the Library of Congress, which states that it knows of no copyright restrictions on it; the 1963 photograph of Wu Chien-Shiung at Columbia comes from the Smithsonian Institution Archives, published with no known copyright restrictions; the photograph of Frances Kelsey receiving her award from President Kennedy comes from the National Library of Medicine, which believes the item to be in the public domain; the April 1936 photograph of Frances Perkins is by Harris & Ewing, held by the Library of Congress, which states that it knows of no copyright restrictions on it; the photograph of Edwin Land presenting at Polaroid is by Bernard Gotfryd, held by the Library of Congress, which states that there are no known restrictions on its publication; the carte de visite of Harriet Tubman, made in Auburn, New York, in 1868 or 1869, is by Benjamin F. Powelson, held by the Library of Congress, which states that there are no known restrictions on its publication; the photograph of Henry Ford, about 1919, is by Fred Hartsook, from the National Photo Company collection at the Library of Congress, which states that there are no known copyright restrictions on its use; the 1897 photograph of Hetty Green is by Hollinger & Rockey, held by the Library of Congress, which states that there are no known restrictions on its publication; the 1936 photograph of Charles Kettering is by Harris & Ewing, held by the Library of Congress, which states that there are no known restrictions on its publication; the 1930s studio portrait of Thomas Midgley Jr. by Blank & Stoller of New York comes from the Science History Institute, which reasonably believes it is not restricted by copyright but says a conclusive determination could not be made; the 1981 photograph of Barbara McClintock holding her Lasker Award and an ear of corn is by Bernard Gotfryd, held by the Library of Congress, which states that there are no known restrictions on its publication; the photograph of Annie Turnbo Malone is from a Poro College souvenir booklet printed between 1920 and 1927, held by the Smithsonian’s National Museum of African American History and Culture, which lists no known copyright restrictions on it; the 1966 photograph of Estée Lauder at a cosmetics counter is by Bill Sauro, a World Journal Tribune staff photograph held by the Library of Congress in its New York World-Telegram & Sun collection, for whose staff photographs the Library states that there are no known restrictions on publication; the portrait of Jay Gould, dated about 1875, is from the George Grantham Bain Collection at the Library of Congress, which states that there are no known restrictions on its publication; the 1937 photograph of Walter Chrysler is by Harris & Ewing, held by the Library of Congress, which states that there are no known restrictions on its publication; the 1896 portrait of Emily Warren Roebling by Carolus-Duran is in the Brooklyn Museum (1994.69.1), which considers it to have no known copyright restrictions; and the photograph of Wilbur Wright of about 1905, attributed to Wilbur or Orville Wright themselves, is held by the Library of Congress, which states that there are no known restrictions on its publication. Everything else came through Wikimedia Commons.

New lives and every correction are also sent by RSS, so a correction reaches a reader who follows the house as surely as a new book does.

Disclosure

This site was assembled by {{EDITOR}} with substantial help from an AI assistant (Anthropic's Claude) — drafting, checking figures against the named sources, and the build itself. The picks, positions and errors are mine; when an error is found it joins the corrections above instead of disappearing. Lines marked “after” a name are compressed notes of someone's idea, not their words, and nobody named on this site has endorsed it or its readings of them. Portraits are public-domain images, except the {{N_LICENSED}} credited above. The page sets no cookies and runs no analytics. Two things are remembered, only in your own browser and never sent anywhere: the Dusk switch (day or dusk), and how far you got in each entry, so it can mark what you have finished and offer to take you back.
